queries.query: In that document sync system, can I stop deletions from spreading to other peers?
queries.answer_note: No — deletes are just entries with Hash::EMPTY and len=0 and propagate through the same sync mechanism; DownloadPolicy only controls whether the content blob downloads, not which entries sync. Deletes are scoped by (author, key_prefix), so one author cannot delete another's entries.
queries.source_summary: An iroh-docs internals answer: no, you cannot disable propagating deletes — deletes are just entries with Hash::EMPTY and len=0 and propagate through the exact same sync mechanism as real entries, with no filtering layer; DownloadPolicy only controls whether the content blob gets downloaded. Deletes are scoped by (author, key_prefix), so an author can only delete entries they themselves wrote.

queries.source_summary: An API answer: yes — doc.set_hash(author_id, key, hash, size) creates an entry pointing to an existing blob by hash without uploading any data; you give it the blake3 hash and size of a blob already in iroh-blobs and it creates a new signed entry — one new entry (~200 bytes of metadata + signatures), zero blob duplication.

queries.query: In that cluster network layout, does machine-to-machine traffic go through the router at all, and what was the simpler wiring suggestion?
queries.answer_note: Intra-cluster traffic is pure ASIC-switched L2 and never touches the router; the router only matters for WAN traffic, and the recommendation is a 40G QSFP+ to 4x10G SFP+ breakout cable directly on one DX010 instead of the small switch.
queries.source_summary: A networking analysis: intra-cluster traffic is pure ASIC-switched L2 (Client A → DX010 → DX010 → Client B) and the router is not in the path — the router only matters for WAN traffic, where its NAT/firewall processing dwarfs the small 10G switch's microseconds; the recommendation is to ditch the small switch and use a 40G QSFP+ → 4x10G SFP+ breakout cable directly on one DX010, gaining 3 spare 10G ports.

queries.query: That single-switch design for the cluster — if the switch itself dies, what actually goes down and what keeps working?
queries.answer_note: Nothing inside the cluster — if the switch dies only WAN dies; the cluster stays up on VLAN 200 through the MC-LAG pair, so there is no point in redundant paths around it (16 ports total: 7 SFP+ 10G and 9 RJ45 1G, all on VLAN 100).
queries.source_summary: A cluster network design note: the switch dying kills WAN only — the cluster stays up on VLAN 200 through the MC-LAG pair, so there is no point in redundant paths around it; everything runs through the one switch (16 ports total: 7 SFP+ 10G for the three Mono nodes and two DX010 breakouts, 9 RJ45 1G in 3G LACP bonds, all on VLAN 100).

queries.query: That router config for the little mono boxes — how are the fast and slow links combined, and which route wins?
queries.answer_note: OpenWrt uses UCI; the design bonds 2x SFP+ 10G as the primary path and 3x RJ45 1G as backup (balance-tlb), with default routes preferring the 10G bond at metric 10 over the 1G bond at metric 100, plus keepalived for the gateway VIP.
queries.source_summary: An OpenWrt configuration: OpenWrt uses UCI for networking; each Mono box bonds 2x SFP+ 10G (bond_sfp, primary) and 3x RJ45 1G (bond_rj45, backup) with bonding_policy balance-tlb, routes prefer the 10G bond (metric 10) over the 1G bond (metric 100), and keepalived runs a VRRP gateway instance with the virtual IP 10.0.100.10.

queries.query: I need copper ethernet out of a cage meant for the bigger optical connectors — that's not a breakout situation, so what's the two-piece trick?
queries.answer_note: A QSA adapter (QSFP+ to SFP+) sits in the cage presenting a single SFP+ slot running one lane at 10G, then a 10GBASE-T SFP+ module plugs into it to give an RJ45 jack — the modules run hot at 2-4W.
queries.source_summary: A networking answer: getting from a QSFP+ cage to an RJ45 jack is a media conversion problem, solved by stacking a QSA adapter (QSFP+ to SFP+, presenting a single SFP+ slot, one lane at 10G) with a 10GBASE-T SFP+ transceiver that provides the RJ45 jack; downsides are the modules run hot (2-4W) and you spend a 40G port on 10G.

queries.query: That NFC reader gotcha from the Japanese bug-hunt — why did flipping the mode in settings leave the chip doing the old thing?
queries.answer_note: UnitST25R3916::config() merely rewrites the cfg struct and is not reflected on the actual chip; you must call configureNFCMode() explicitly on every mode change (switching NFC-F to NFC-B by config() alone left the chip in the old mode).
queries.source_summary: A cross-verified research report on M5Unit-NFC issues records the key gotcha: UnitST25R3916::config() does not touch hardware — it merely rewrites the cfg struct and is only applied when configureNFCMode() is called (which happens once inside begin()); switching NFC-F/NFC-B by calling config() alone left the chip in the old mode, so configureNFCMode() must be called explicitly on every mode change.

queries.query: That encrypted key file for the virtualization secrets — I was about to just delete it. Why is that the wrong move, and what's the safer equivalent?
queries.answer_note: It is a systemd-creds-encrypted blob libvirt uses for its own stored secrets — but the host key that could open it is already gone, so it is undecryptable either way; deleting gains nothing and blocks regeneration, so move it aside instead (identical effect on the service's condition check, fully reversible).
queries.source_summary: An analysis of /var/lib/libvirt/secrets/secrets-encryption-key: a systemd-creds-encrypted blob generated by virt-secret-init-encryption.service that libvirt uses to encrypt its own stored secrets at rest. There are no secrets to protect (the directory holds only the key file, no VMs defined), and the host key /var/lib/systemd/credential.secret that could open the blob is gone, so it is already undecryptable — deleting it only blocks regeneration (the service skips itself while the file exists); moving it aside has the identical effect and is reversible.

queries.query: does that pool setting in the tool daemon cap how many clients can connect at once
queries.answer_note: No — pool.max limits copies of an MCP server process, not the number of clients; a shared process can serve multiple clients and calls. queries.source_summary: A Q&A answer: pool.max = 4 limits copies of an MCP server process, not the number of clients — a shared process can serve multiple clients and calls; if a server is configured for separate processes per session, mcpx can run up to four copies for that pool and callers needing another copy wait for capacity; a global-scope server is limited to one copy regardless of the setting; a per-server max can override the daemon-wide pool.max.

queries.query: In that signed-artifact system, can somebody tag an artifact they didn't create, and what exactly does a signature cover?
queries.answer_note: Yes — every artifact is signed by the key that created it, and a tag is that key's claim about another artifact; the subject's author plays no part (a cosign would be a tag pointing at the original by hash). Verification rebuilds the record and re-serializes with serde_json (sorted keys), so the signature covers the re-serialization, not the wire bytes.
queries.source_summary: Design answers: anyone can tag anything — every artifact is signed by the key that created it and a tag is that key's claim about another artifact, the subject's author plays no part (the design doc saying otherwise is wrong). No one can add a signature to another's artifact; a cosign is a tag pointing at the original by hash. The signature is a field on every artifact; receivers rebuild {author, seq, prev, kind, body, after} and serialize with serde_json (default map is sorted, preserve_order off), so the signature covers that re-serialization, not the bytes that arrived.

queries.query: That correction at the top of the comparison — the other stack turned out not to have the history-limited encryption at all, and its famous group-size number was not a limit. Explain both.
queries.answer_note: It does not: p2panda's Data Encryption keeps one group key, rotates on removal, and gives every past epoch key to new members (so late joiners read all history); the causal encryption is Keyhive's. The 128 figure was a performance observation about DCGKA group sizes, not a cap.
queries.source_summary: A corrections note: p2panda has no causal encryption — its Data Encryption keeps one group key, rotates it on removal, and gives every past epoch key to new members, so a late joiner can read all history; the causal encryption is Keyhive's. And the 128 figure was the author's error: the p2panda blog calls DCGKA 'performant for small- to mid-size groups of ca. 128 members' — a performance observation, not a hard cap.

queries.query: That edge webhook gateway — how does it treat a delivery with a bad signature, and what guarantees does a good delivery get?
queries.answer_note: The gateway verifies X-Hub-Signature-256 (HMAC-SHA-256, timing-safe) and writes nothing on a bad signature (401, no R2 object, no ledger row — proven in acceptance tests with a forged all-zeros signature). Valid payloads are stored verbatim in R2, ledgered in D1 as pending, and delivered via a queue with exponential-backoff retries; rows are never dropped and there is no 'failed' terminal state — pending is the durable state during an outage, with a 5-minute cron sweeper re-enqueueing stale rows oldest-first and an admin replay endpoint.
queries.source_summary: A build/acceptance report and the operator README agree: the Worker verifies X-Hub-Signature-256 (HMAC-SHA-256, timing-safe compare) against GITHUB_SECRET — bad signature → 401 and nothing is written (verified: no R2 object, ledger row count unchanged). Raw bodies are stored verbatim in R2 (github/<delivery-id>.json), a D1 deliveries row is written as pending, and a queue consumer delivers with exponential backoff (1m → 30m cap); rows are never dropped and there is no failed terminal state — pending is the durable state; a cron sweeper every 5 min re-enqueues stale pending rows oldest-first, and POST /admin/replay force-replays all pending in received order. Acceptance: 4 queued deliveries replayed in exact received order; forged signature rejected.

queries.query: That daemon takeover work — what is the safety rule for handing a live connection to the new process, and when is the old process allowed to exit?
queries.answer_note: A connection is passed only if no byte has been read from it since the server last wrote to it (the first idle-reset rule failed about once in twenty runs with a 405, because net/http background-reads one byte into its hasByte buffer). Frozen sockets are duplicated and sent one descriptor per frame via SCM_RIGHTS, the old side closes its copies only after the successor commits — the commit reply is the point of no return — and the old process exits only after the successor closes the connection, which is after it has sent MAINPID.
queries.source_summary: The takeover design doc (repo-docs) states the read rule: a connection is passed only if no byte has been read from it since the server last wrote to it; the first rule (resetting the 'taken' flag at idle) failed once in twenty stress runs with a 405 because net/http background-reads a byte into hasByte while a handler runs. Frozen sockets are duplicated close-on-exec and sent with SCM_RIGHTS, one descriptor per frame, and the old side closes its copies only after the successor commits; on failure before commit the frozen connections are thawed and keep-alives keep working. An opencode session chunk adds the protocol points: the old side keeps duplicate listener fds until the successor commits, sends one fd per message and waits for an ack so fds can't coalesce, only the successor's commit reply moves the old side past the point of no return, and the old process exits only after the successor closes the connection, which is after it has sent MAINPID.

queries.query: That tiered-vector design and the search reference agree on a hard rule about mixing — state it from both sides.
queries.answer_note: A vector set is a point in (model, width, quantization, chunking profile) space, stored in its own vec_<model>_<width>_<quant> table over the same canonical chunks; sets are mutually incompatible — a query vector from one model can only search that model's set, and nothing is ever mixed within a set. On the query side, the operator class and the query operator must be a matched pair for the distance metric (cosine: vector_cosine_ops with <=>; L2: vector_l2_ops with <->; inner product: vector_ip_ops with <#>), and stored and query embeddings must use the same model and preprocessing.

The vector-search reference: choose the operator class and query operator as a matched pair (cosine/vector_cosine_ops/<=>, L2/vector_l2_ops/<->, inner product/vector_ip_ops/<#>), and generate stored-document and query embeddings with the same model and preprocessing.

queries.answer_note: No — intra-cluster traffic is pure ASIC-switched L2 through the DX010s and never touches the router (the router only matters for WAN); the Mono gateways bond 2x SFP+ 10G as primary and 3x RJ45 1G as backup (balance-tlb), with default routes preferring the 10G bond at metric 10 over the 1G bond at metric 100.

queries.query: Two crypto designs from the identity work — how does the identity store plan to derive its keys, and what does the topic-tracker library expose for signing and encryption?

The topic-tracker crate exposes encryption_keypair and signing_keypair with a RecordPublisher holding an Ed25519 signing key and optional secret rotation — and it is pinned to iroh 0.95, incompatible with iroh-gossip 0.96.

An API reference for distributed-topic-tracker: crypto module exports DefaultSecretRotation, EncryptedRecord, RecordPublisher, encryption_keypair and signing_keypair; the crate pins iroh/iroh-gossip 0.95 and is not compatible with iroh-gossip 0.96.

queries.query: That editor auto-save design shows up in both a plan and the validated design doc — what bug did it fix, and how does it respect the server's save rate limit?
queries.answer_note: Both the implementation plan and the validated design agree: saves were manual-only and the save button stayed permanently disabled after the first save (disabled set, never re-enabled) — the fix is a state-machine AutoSaveManager with a 2-second debounce after the last edit, and because the server enforces a 5-second cooldown per filename (HTTP 429), the client parses the retry delay from the response, shows 'retry…', and retries after the delay plus a 500 ms buffer; a NewVersion from another client cancels pending auto-save timers.
queries.source_summary: An implementation plan and the validated design doc for 'Auto-save on idle' describe the same work: saves are manual-only (button + Ctrl+S) and the save button stays permanently disabled after the first save because disabled = true is set but never re-enabled; the solution is a state-machine-driven AutoSaveManager in main.ts (2s debounce via AUTOSAVE_DEBOUNCE_MS = 2000), client-side only, respecting the server's 5-second rate limit per filename (HTTP 429) by parsing 'Save rate limited. Try again in Xs.' and retrying after the delay + RATE_LIMIT_BUFFER_MS = 500; a NewVersion from collab cancels pending timers and marks state saved.

queries.query: What did the hardware digging establish about that e-reader's keyboard link and its charging limits?
queries.answer_note: The keyboard link is one-way only because of firmware: the 6-pin inter-board connector physically carries both USART2_RX and USART2_TX (2× 3V3, 2× GND), so bidirectional comms need no hardware change. On charging, the breakout board holds a 350 mA PTC fuse which caps charge current regardless of what the charger chip could deliver — and the charger analysis (from the programming resistors) gives ICHG = 2.00 A (R25 = 20 kΩ) and VBATREG = 4.18 V, with no thermistor on TS, so battery temperature is not monitored.
queries.source_summary: Seed (a hardware-mining report): the breakout board does have a full schematic; the keyboard↔main 6-pin connector carries 2× 3V3, USART2_RX, USART2_TX, 2× GND — the RX line physically exists, only firmware makes the link one-way, so bidirectional comms need no hardware change; the main↔breakout 16-pin connector carries USB D± and SD SPI, and the breakout holds a 350 mA PTC fuse which caps charge current regardless of what the BQ25306 could deliver. Partner (a BQ25306 charger README research report): both programming resistors solved — R25 = 20 kΩ → ICHG = 40000/20000 = 2.00 A; R29/R28 give VBATREG = 1.1 × 3.8 = 4.18 V; TS has no thermistor (R17/R18 10k/10k is TI's documented 'unused' network), so battery temperature is not monitored.

queries.query: What did the measurements say about the cost of the default way of welcoming a new group member, in both the spike results and the design doc?
queries.answer_note: About 146 B per epoch secret (146.6 B stock per epoch in the spike), so the welcome grows linearly — about 147 KB at 1,000 epochs/rotations; the serde_bytes change cuts it to roughly 40 B per secret but is wire-incompatible, so it needs a new scheme version.

queries.query: The friendship design shows up in both a code summary and a design review — how is the two-member limit actually enforced, since the underlying auth library can't carry it?
queries.answer_note: It is an ingest rewrite: p2panda-auth's ignore set cannot carry the cap, so an over-cap add is turned into a no-op at ingest; dissolve is a projection (an effective removal of either member ends the friendship), and in the friendship module a removal naming the same request beats a concurrent accept.
queries.source_summary: The friendship module summary: friendship forms from a request, each account capped at MAX_FRIENDS (100), removal wins over a concurrent accept naming the same request. The design review states the enforcement: the two-member cap is ours — p2panda-auth's ignore set cannot carry it, so the cap is an ingest rewrite that turns an over-cap add into a no-op; dissolve is a projection, where an effective removal of either member ends the friendship.

queries.query: Two different crypto pieces for the identity platform were evaluated — what did the envelope work conclude about rotation, and what did the group-key spike find about people who join late?
queries.answer_note: Keyhive envelopes rotate their key material on every publish, with format versioning deliberately deferred; and the BeeKEM spike found a join hands over a copy of roughly the whole state that leaks old epoch keys — the joiner can derive the epoch-0 root even though it was not a member then (no forward secrecy).
queries.source_summary: A Keyhive research chunk concludes envelopes rotate key material per publish and format versioning is deferred. The BeeKEM spike RESULTS doc finds: a join gives the joiner a replica copy of about the whole state (growing with history); the joiner derives the current root AND the epoch-0 root though it was not a member then — a copy leaks old epoch keys, and there is no forward secrecy against removed/compromised members in the tested cases.

queries.answer_note: The DGM must insert the joiner on welcome, because the upstream path overwrites it: Dcgka::add clones the adder's DGM before the add is applied and process_welcome overwrites the joiner's DGM with that copy, so the joiner is never added.

The design review states the requirement: DGM is ours, and the DGM must insert the joiner on welcome, because the upstream path overwrites it.

queries.query: Across the worlds work, what's the default sharing posture between worlds, and how are the permission tokens supposed to evolve?
queries.answer_note: Every world is fully isolated by default; an admin/moderator-level mode can set specific worlds to unisolated so they can share or access across worlds. Capabilities are staged: Stage 0 (now) is server-held bearer capabilities, digest-stored and attenuable inside one server; signed capabilities and delegation chains arrive at Stage 1 only when a capability must be checkable offline or handed to a party that shouldn't reach the server; Keyhive is deferred until it reaches a stable release.
queries.source_summary: Seed (a session continuation summary): the request adds a per-world isolation mode, default isolated, that an admin/moderator can set to unisolated for specific worlds to share or access across worlds. Partner (attenuated-capabilities design doc): Stage 0 (v1, now) is server-held bearer capabilities, digest-stored, attenuable inside one server with the ceiling as policy; Stage 1 (triggered when a capability must be checkable without the issuing server online) adds signed capabilities and delegation chains; Stage 2 evaluates Keyhive, which is pre-alpha and adopted only behind the Stage 1 verifier after a stable release.

queries.query: That contact-naming feature for the identity tool — where do the names live, and what stops somebody impersonating a contact?
queries.answer_note: Petnames are per owner and live in their own append-only journal (petnames.jsonl beside directory.jsonl), never replicated. A petname must be unique per owner in both directions, and mimicry is refused — folded or confusable matches with another contact's petname or an account's alleged name are rejected. An invite's key is the account ID, so confirming an invite sets a petname for exactly the issuing account; the display fingerprint is the first 6 hex characters of the account ID.
queries.source_summary: Seed (a subagent commit report on feat/id-petnames, commit 89427074): petnames are per owner and live in their own journal, never replicated; a petname must be unique per owner in both directions and mimicry is refused (folded or confusable matches rejected); fingerprint is the first 6 hex characters of the account ID; an invite's key is the account ID so confirming sets a petname for exactly the issuing account; store location petnames.jsonl beside directory.jsonl, append-only. Partner (the feature design doc) states the same decisions: petnames.jsonl not in the directory journal so petnames are never replicated; mimicry refused for exact (folded) and confusable matches; invite key is the account ID.
